q-162412.name: Question 1
q-162412.problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=-1,$ $x=1,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=2xz\,i+({x}^{2}+z)\,j+2\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
q-162412.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2) \\  & =2z+0+0 \\  & =2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2z\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2z\,\text{d}z \\  & =(1-(-1))\cdot (1-0)\cdot [{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1} \\  & =2({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162576.name: Question 2
q-162576.problem: Consider the positively (outward) oriented surface $S$ given by $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z+3)^{2}=16$ and the vector field $F=(x+2y)\,i+(4z-y)\,j+(z+xy)\,k.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
q-162576.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4z-y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z+xy) \\  & =1+(-1)+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid sphere of radius $4$ enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}1\,\text{d}V \\  & =1{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & ={∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =\text{Volume}(R) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {4}^{3} \\  & =\frac{256\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162582.name: Question 3
q-162582.problem: Consider the positively (outward) oriented surface $S$ given by $(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=36$ and the vector field $F=(x+1)\,i-y\,j+z\,k.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
q-162582.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z) \\  & =1+(-1)+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid sphere of radius $6$ enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}1\,\text{d}V \\  & =1{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =1\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {6}^{3} \\  & =288\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

q-162598.name: Question 4
q-162598.problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $y=0,$ $y=\pi ,$ $z=2,$ $z=4.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F={z}^{3}\,i+2xz\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j+x{y}^{2}\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
q-162598.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xz\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =0+(-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+0 \\  & =-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}(-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}(-2xz\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{2}^{4}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot [\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{y=0}^{y=\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=2}^{z=4} \\  & =({1}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\cdot (\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot (-2)\cdot 6 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162603.name: Question 5
q-162603.problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=1,$ $x=4,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=1,$ $z=2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=y\sqrt{x}\,i+(z-x)\,j+{y}^{3}\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
q-162603.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\sqrt{x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-x)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}}+0+0 \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{y}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}\text{d}z \\  & =[\sqrt{x}]_{x=1}^{x=4}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\cdot (2-1) \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
